intro: Hurling is an ancient Irish field game played with an ash stick (the hurley or camán) and a small leather ball (the sliotar). Players strike the sliotar huge distances through the air, catch it in their hand and race along balancing it on the hurley. Goals can be scored under the crossbar or points over it. The Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) runs the game; the women's equivalent is camogie.
inThirtySeconds: Under the crossbar into the net: a goal, worth 3 points.
Over the bar between the posts: a point.
You may catch the sliotar, but carry it in the hand for no more than four steps.
To run further, balance or bounce it on the hurley — the 'solo run'.
objective: Outscore the opponent with goals and points; scores are written like 2–15 (2 goals, 15 points = 21).

facts.environment: Large grass pitch with H-shaped goals

scoring.label: Goal
scoring.detail: Sliotar enters the net under the crossbar.

scoring.label: Point
scoring.detail: Sliotar passes over the crossbar between the posts.

bodies.name: Gaelic Athletic Association
bodies.scope: Governing body for hurling and Gaelic football

rules.title: Four steps in hand
rules.summary: A player may catch the sliotar and carry it in the hand for no more than four steps.
rules.body: After that, the player must strike it, hand-pass it, or play it onto the hurley. The ball may be returned to the hand only a limited number of times during a run before it must be released.

rules.title: The solo run
rules.summary: Players run with the sliotar balanced or bouncing on the bas (the flat end) of the hurley.
rules.body: There's no limit to how far you can carry it on the hurley — making the solo run one of hurling's signature skills.

rules.title: No picking up off the ground
rules.summary: The sliotar may not be picked up directly from the ground with the hand; it must be lifted with the hurley.
rules.body: Players flick the ball up with the hurley ('jab lift' or 'roll lift') before catching it.

rules.title: Goals and points
rules.summary: Into the net under the bar: a goal (3). Over the bar between the posts: a point (1).
rules.body: The total is written goals–points, so 1–20 (23) beats 3–12 (21). A goal may not be thrown or hand-passed into the net. Competitions occasionally trial scoring changes, so check the current GAA rules.
rules.example: A team scores 2 goals and 18 points: '2–18', a total of 24.

rules.title: Puck-outs and frees
rules.summary: After a score or a wide, the goalkeeper restarts with a puck-out from the small rectangle; fouls give a free puck.
rules.body: Free-takers strike from the ground using a lift and strike. A '65' (from the 65 m line) is awarded when the defending team plays the ball over its own end line.

rules.title: Fair and foul contact
rules.summary: Shoulder-to-shoulder contact is allowed when contesting the ball; striking, pulling or tripping an opponent is a foul.
rules.body: Dangerous use of the hurley (high swings, striking the hand) is severely punished. Referees use yellow, black and red cards depending on the offence.

fouls.name: Overcarrying
fouls.description: More than four steps with the sliotar in hand.

fouls.name: Picking up off the ground
fouls.description: Lifting the ball with the hand.

fouls.name: Pulling across
fouls.description: Swinging the hurley into an opponent.

flow.title: Throw-in
flow.description: The referee throws the sliotar in between midfielders.

flow.title: End-to-end play
flow.description: Long strikes, high catches and solo runs.

flow.title: Full-time
flow.description: Draws may go to extra time or replays depending on the competition.

positions.name: Goalkeeper
positions.role: Guards the net and takes puck-outs.

positions.name: Midfield
positions.role: Two players covering the whole pitch.

positions.name: Half-forward line and full-forward line
positions.role: Six attackers aiming for goals and points.

field.name: Pitch
notes: Same pitch and goals as Gaelic football
Lines at 13 m, 20 m and 65 m

glossary.definition: The flat striking end of the hurley.

funFacts: Hurling is recognised by UNESCO as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
Inter-county hurlers are amateurs, despite crowds of more than 80,000 at Croke Park.
